case_prompt: A 37-year-old man was admitted in early November 2014 with intermittent fevers of one month’s duration, peaking at 39.6°C, accompanied by night sweats, mild cough, and a 7-kg weight loss over two months. Initial mycobacterial studies were negative, and a bone marrow smear showed yeast-like organisms, but culture was unrevealing. He received moxifloxacin for ten days and voriconazole for three days without improvement. He worked in a blood bank with frequent plasma donation and had recent soil exposure through farm work in his home region along the Yangtze River; he had never traveled abroad. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C), tachycardic, and ill-appearing, with no lymphadenopathy, but hepatomegaly (2 cm below the costal margin) and splenomegaly (3 cm below the costal margin). Laboratory studies revealed progressive pancytopenia (WBC 1.86 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 86 g/L, platelets 2 × 10^9/L), elevated C-reactive protein (43 mg/L), abnormal liver enzymes, low CD4 count (320 cells/μL), and positive CMV IgM and HSV antibodies; HIV serology, PPD, and T-SPOT were negative. Blood and sputum cultures were repeatedly negative. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly with retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy; chest CT showed only minimal chronic inflammation. PET-CT revealed increased glucose uptake in bone marrow and spleen without evidence of malignancy. He was treated with ganciclovir for ten days and received supportive IVIG and thymalfasin, but fever and cytopenias persisted with further hepatosplenomegaly.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Lymphoma was considered but excluded — “PET‐CT revealed no malignant tumour, excluding lymphoma.” 2. Tuberculosis was considered but excluded — “no pathogenic evidence of tuberculosis was found, and the PPD and T‐SPOT results were negative.” 3. Penicilliosis was considered in the differential of systemic mycoses — “histoplasmosis and penicilliosis have similar clinical presentations, laboratory findings, and chest radiographic abnormalities… thus, these two kinds of microorganisms should be microbiologically distinguished.”

selection.screen_reason: Prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia with soil exposure in the Yangtze region and yeast forms in marrow make disseminated histoplasmosis reachable.
selection.second_look_note: Prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia with soil exposure from farm work in the Yangtze region and yeast forms in marrow; the exposure history matters.
